blocks.prompt: How the Teddy Bear Got Its Name
blocks.text: Over a hundred years ago, the president of the United States was named Theodore Roosevelt. Everyone called him Teddy. One day he went on a bear hunt in Mississippi. He looked for days and found nothing. So the other men found a bear for him and tied it to a tree. They told him to shoot it. Roosevelt said no. He said it was not fair to shoot a bear that could not get away. A man drew the story as a cartoon in the newspaper, and people all over the country saw it. A shop owner in New York saw it too. He made a small stuffed bear and put it in his shop window. He called it Teddy's bear. That is how the teddy bear got its name.

blocks.prompt: The Bear the President Would Not Shoot
blocks.text: In November 1902, President Theodore Roosevelt traveled to Mississippi to hunt bears. Everyone called him Teddy, though he did not like the nickname one bit. The hunt went badly. For days the president tramped through the woods and found nothing at all. His guide was a famous tracker named Holt Collier. Collier finally cornered a black bear and tied it to a willow tree, then sent word for the president to come and take the shot. Roosevelt refused. Shooting an animal that could not run away was not hunting, he said. It would not be fair, and it would not count. A newspaper cartoonist named Clifford Berryman heard the story and drew it for the Washington Post. In the cartoon, the president stands with his back turned and his hand raised, and behind him sits a small, frightened bear. People loved that drawing. In Brooklyn, a shop owner named Morris Michtom saw it in the paper. His wife Rose sewed a little stuffed bear out of soft cloth, and they set it in their shop window next to a copy of the cartoon. Beside it they put a sign: Teddy's bear. It sold. So did the next one, and the next.

blocks.prompt: Two Bears, One Year
blocks.text:
The teddy bear has two origin stories, and the strange part is that both are true. They happened on opposite sides of an ocean within months of each other, and neither inventor had ever heard of the other.

The American story starts with a bad hunting trip. In November 1902, President Theodore Roosevelt spent days in the Mississippi woods without finding a bear. His guide finally cornered one and tied it to a tree so the president could take an easy shot. Roosevelt refused. A cartoonist named Clifford Berryman drew the moment for the Washington Post, and the picture spread across the country. A Brooklyn shopkeeper named Morris Michtom saw it. His wife Rose sewed a small plush bear, and they set it in the window beside a copy of the cartoon with a label reading Teddy's bear. Customers wanted one. Then they wanted thousands. The Michtoms went on to build the Ideal Toy Company.

The German story starts with a woman named Margarete Steiff. Polio had left her unable to walk, and she ran a small felt workshop in the town of Giengen, sewing toy elephants and other animals. Her nephew Richard studied art, and he spent his free hours at a zoo in Stuttgart with a sketchbook, drawing real bears. He wanted a toy bear whose arms and legs actually moved, so he designed one with jointed limbs. The company carried it to the Leipzig toy fair in 1903. Nobody was interested. On the last day, an American buyer walked past, stopped, and ordered three thousand of them.

Two bears, one year, no connection at all. The name came from the American story. The design came from the German one. Almost every teddy bear made since is some mixture of the two.

blocks.prompt: The Bear With a Job
blocks.text:
Ask an adult what a teddy bear is for and they will probably say it is for playing with. That is not quite right. Watch a two-year-old with a well-loved bear and you will notice it is rarely a toy in the ordinary sense. It is not raced, stacked, or built with. It is carried. It gets held during the parts of the day that are hard: leaving the house, sitting in a waiting room, falling asleep in a dark bedroom.

In 1953, a British pediatrician named Donald Winnicott gave that behavior a name. He called objects like the bear transitional objects, and he argued they do serious work. A baby begins life unable to tell where it stops and its mother starts. Learning that other people are separate is a real achievement, and it is frightening. The bear, Winnicott suggested, sits in that gap. It is the first thing a child owns that is clearly not part of the child and clearly not a parent either. It is a rehearsal for being alone.

Winnicott also noticed that these objects follow rules, and the rules are strict. The bear has to be soft, and it has to keep a texture the child knows by heart. It has to survive being adored and being thrown across the room. Above all, nobody else is allowed to change it. This is why washing a child's bear can go so badly wrong. To an adult, a wash is care. To the child, the smell was part of the bear, and a parent has quietly swapped in a stranger.

Hospitals took the idea seriously. Since the 1990s, medical students across Europe have run teddy bear hospitals. Children bring in their bears, explain what is wrong, and watch a bandage go on. The child is not the patient. The bear is. Nothing frightening happens to anybody, and that is exactly the point. A child who has watched a stethoscope press against a bear's chest is a child less afraid of the one coming toward their own.

The teddy bear began as a joke about a president who would not take an unfair shot. It became something odder and more useful: a soft, patient, slightly grubby machine for practicing courage.

notes: Roosevelt hunt: Mississippi, November 1902

Snouts shrank, foreheads grew, decade after decade

blocks.prompt: How the Teddy Bear Lost Its Snout
blocks.text:
Set a teddy bear from 1903 beside one bought last week and the difference is impossible to miss. The old bear has a long pointed snout, a hump behind its shoulders, small eyes set high on the skull, and long dangling limbs. It looks like a bear. The new one has a flat face, a round head, and large eyes set low and wide apart. It looks like a baby.

Nothing about this was planned. No committee met to redesign the bear. It happened the way a species changes: slowly, through millions of small decisions, each one made by somebody who was not thinking about the century.

In 1985, the Cambridge biologist Robert Hinde and his colleague L. A. Barden decided to measure it. Hinde studied animal behavior for a living, and he treated the teddy bear as though it were a population under study. He and Barden collected bears made across eight decades and took the same measurements from each: the length of the snout, the height of the forehead. The trend was clear and it ran one way. Decade after decade, the snout got shorter and the forehead got taller. The bear was drifting steadily toward the proportions of an infant.

There is a name for those proportions. In 1943, the Austrian zoologist Konrad Lorenz described what he called the baby schema: a large head on a small body, a bulging forehead, big low-set eyes, round cheeks. Human beings, Lorenz argued, respond to that shape automatically, with a rush of tenderness they do not choose and cannot easily switch off. It works on puppies. It works on cartoon characters. In 1979 Stephen Jay Gould pointed out that Mickey Mouse had done exactly the same thing across fifty years, growing a bigger head and larger eyes and shedding his rat-like snout, without Disney ever announcing a redesign.

So the teddy bear had been selected. The selective pressure was a shopper's hand reaching for one bear instead of another, repeated across generations. Babyish bears sold. Bears that looked like actual bears sat on the shelf. The manufacturer read the sales figures, nudged the pattern, and the process ran again.

Here is the part of the study almost everyone forgets. Hinde and Barden also showed bears to children and asked which they preferred. Children under four did not prefer the baby-faced bears at all. The preference only appeared in older children, around age eight and above. The animal reshaped by love was not being reshaped by the people who loved it most. Toddlers, the actual users, had no vote. The face of the modern teddy bear was chosen by adults and older children buying gifts, projecting onto a toy what they assumed a small child would want.

That is worth sitting with. A century of design driven by a preference belonging to somebody other than the customer. The bear got softer-faced every decade because the person paying was moved by soft faces, and nobody ever asked the two-year-old.

The origin story has the same shape. Roosevelt refused to shoot a bear that had been tied to a tree, and Berryman's cartoon turned that refusal into an image of mercy. The full account is harsher. The animal was old and badly injured by the time the president arrived, and Roosevelt ordered it killed with a knife to end its suffering. That part never made the cartoon. What survived was the gentler version, because the gentler version was the one people wanted to keep. The bear on the shelf has been shaped by the same instinct, all the way down.
